interactions.label: Why do plain polysaccharide vaccines fail to protect infants under two years of

params.question: Why do plain polysaccharide vaccines fail to protect infants under two years of age?

answers.text: Infant B lymphocytes lack surface receptors for polysaccharide antigens and cannot mount any response

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Infant B cells do possess surface receptors and can bind polysaccharides. The problem is that without T-cell help, the response produces only short-lived IgM and no memory B cells.

answers.text: Maternal IgG transferred across the placenta neutralises the polysaccharide before it can stimulate infant B cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Although maternal IgG can interfere with certain live vaccines, it is not the reason polysaccharide vaccines fail. The failure occurs because polysaccharides are T-independent and cannot generate memory, regardless of maternal antibody levels.

answers.text: Polysaccharides are thymus-independent antigens that produce only IgM with no class switching or memory

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Polysaccharide antigens bypass T cells entirely, producing only short-lived IgM with no class switching or memory. Conjugate vaccines link the polysaccharide to a carrier protein, converting it into a T-dependent antigen that recruits T-cell help and generates lasting immunity — which is why Hib and PCV protect infants.

answers.text: The infant thymus has not matured enough to process and present polysaccharide antigens to T helper cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The issue is not thymic immaturity — it is that polysaccharide antigens are inherently T-independent and bypass T cells entirely. Even in adults with a fully mature thymus, polysaccharides alone cannot recruit T-cell help.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the T-dependent vs T-independent distinction. Polysaccharides bypass T cells, producing only IgM without memory. Conjugate vaccines solve this by attaching a carrier protein that recruits T-cell help, enabling class switching and lasting immunity.
Well done. This T-dependent vs T-independent distinction underpins the rationale for conjugate vaccines in the paediatric immunisation schedule.

interactions.label: Why does advanced HIV infection lead to reactivation of latent tuberculosis?

params.question: Why does advanced HIV infection lead to reactivation of latent tuberculosis?

answers.text: HIV directly destroys alveolar macrophages, releasing dormant mycobacteria from granulomas

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. HIV does not directly destroy alveolar macrophages. The mechanism is loss of CD4+ Th1 cells, which are needed to produce interferon-gamma and maintain macrophage activation against intracellular mycobacteria.

answers.text: HIV reduces CD4+ T cell counts, impairing the Th1-driven macrophage activation that contains M. tuberculosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. M. tuberculosis survives inside macrophages and is held in check by Th1-driven interferon-gamma activation. HIV selectively destroys CD4+ T cells, collapsing this cell-mediated containment. Without sustained Th1 signalling, macrophages can no longer suppress the dormant bacilli, leading to reactivation.

answers.text: HIV produces antibodies that cross-react with mycobacterial cell wall components, enhancing bacterial growth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. HIV does not produce cross-reactive antibodies against mycobacteria. TB reactivation occurs because CD4+ T cell depletion removes the Th1 cell-mediated control that keeps M. tuberculosis contained in granulomas.

answers.text: HIV suppresses neutrophil oxidative burst, removing the primary killing mechanism against mycobacteria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While the neutrophil oxidative burst is critical in some infections (e.g., Chronic Granulomatous Disease), mycobacterial containment depends primarily on CD4+ Th1 cells activating macrophages through interferon-gamma, not on neutrophils.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: M. tuberculosis is an intracellular pathogen controlled by Th1 cells activating macrophages via interferon-gamma. HIV destroys CD4+ T cells, collapsing this arm and enabling TB reactivation.
Exactly right. The HIV–TB connection illustrates why cell-mediated immunity is indispensable against intracellular pathogens.

interactions.label: The Mantoux tuberculin skin test works by detecting anti-mycobacterial antibodie

params.question: The Mantoux tuberculin skin test works by detecting anti-mycobacterial antibodies at the injection site.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect — the Mantoux test measures cell-mediated immunity, not antibodies. It is a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction: sensitised Th1 cells recognise tuberculin and release interferon-gamma, activating macrophages and producing induration over 48–72 hours. No immunoglobulin is involved in this reaction.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the Mantoux test does not detect antibodies. It is a Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction: previously sensitised CD4+ Th1 cells recognise tuberculin, release interferon-gamma, and recruit macrophages to the site. The resulting induration at 48–72 hours reflects cell-mediated immunity, not humoral.

interactions.label: A nurse who previously tolerated penicillin develops anaphylaxis on re-exposure.

params.question: A nurse who previously tolerated penicillin develops anaphylaxis on re-exposure. Why does the second exposure trigger a life-threatening reaction while the first did not?

answers.text: Complement proteins accumulate after the first exposure and lyse the nurse's own cells on re-exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Complement-mediated lysis features in Type II and III hypersensitivity. Type I anaphylaxis is driven by IgE on mast cells, not by complement accumulation.

answers.text: The first exposure generated IgE that armed mast cells; re-exposure cross-links this IgE, triggering massive histamine release

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The first exposure to penicillin (acting as a hapten bound to serum proteins) stimulated IgE production. This IgE armed mast cells throughout the body. On re-exposure, penicillin cross-links the bound IgE, causing immediate mast cell degranulation and massive histamine release — the hallmark of Type I hypersensitivity.

answers.text: Immune complexes formed during the first exposure deposited in tissues and activated neutrophils on re-exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Immune complex deposition describes Type III hypersensitivity, which develops over hours, not minutes. The immediate onset of anaphylaxis indicates Type I (IgE-mediated).

answers.text: Sensitised CD8+ T cells from the first exposure attack penicillin-exposed tissues on re-exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. CD8+ T cell–mediated responses describe Type IV delayed hypersensitivity, which takes 24–72 hours to develop. The immediate onset within minutes rules out T-cell involvement.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is timing and mechanism: Type I = IgE on mast cells (minutes), Type II = IgG/IgM on cells (hours), Type III = immune complexes (hours), Type IV = T cells (24–72 hours). Anaphylaxis within minutes points to Type I.
Well done. Understanding that IgE sensitisation requires initial exposure and that anaphylaxis occurs only on re-exposure is key to recognising Type I hypersensitivity.

params.question: Six weeks after receiving a kidney transplant, a patient develops fever and rising serum creatinine. Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltration of the graft. What is the most likely type of rejection and its mechanism?

answers.text: Hyperacute rejection caused by preformed anti-donor antibodies destroying the graft vasculature

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes of transplantation when preformed antibodies attack the graft vasculature. The onset at six weeks with lymphocytic infiltrate indicates a T-cell mediated process, not preformed antibody.

answers.text: Chronic rejection caused by gradual fibrosis from indirect processing of donor HLA fragments by host cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Chronic rejection develops over months to years through the indirect pathway, where host antigen-presenting cells process donor HLA fragments. The timeline of six weeks and the dense lymphocytic infiltrate are characteristic of acute rejection.

answers.text: Graft-versus-host disease caused by donor lymphocytes attacking recipient tissues

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Graft-versus-host disease involves donor immune cells attacking the recipient's tissues, typically seen in bone marrow transplants. In solid organ transplants, rejection is host-versus-graft, with recipient T cells attacking the donor organ.

answers.text: Acute rejection caused by host T cells directly recognising intact donor HLA molecules on graft cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Acute rejection typically occurs days to weeks after transplantation. Host T cells directly recognise intact donor HLA molecules on graft cells (the direct pathway), leading to lymphocytic infiltration and graft damage. Cyclosporin prevents this by blocking calcineurin and inhibiting IL-2 production, suppressing T-cell activation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Three rejection types are distinguished by timing and mechanism: hyperacute (minutes, preformed antibodies), acute (days to weeks, T cells recognising donor HLA directly), and chronic (months to years, indirect processing causing fibrosis). This case points to acute rejection.

Well done. The direct pathway — host T cells recognising donor HLA — drives acute rejection, while the indirect pathway drives chronic fibrosis. Timing and biopsy findings distinguish the three types.
